Assessment of the aerobic preparation and bottom ash addition
as pretreatment steps before landﬁlling: Impact on methanogenesis kinetics
and leachate parameters
Alicia A. Mansour a,⇑, Antoine Motte a, Virginie Pallier b, Geneviève Feuillade-Cathalifaud b,
Arnaud Ponthieux a
a Veolia Environnement Recherche et Innovation (VERI), 291 avenue Dreyfous Ducas, Zone portuaire de Limay, 78520 Limay, France
b University of Limoges, GRESE, ENSIL, Parc d’ESTER Technopôle, 16 rue Atlantis, 87068 Limoges Cedex, France

This work focuses on assessing the impact of two types of waste pretreatment: addition of bottom ashes
and aerobic pretreatment on both the onset and kinetics of methanogenesis and the evolution of different
parameters in the leachate. It also studies the correlation between methane production and the different
parameters measured in the leachate produced. A total of six 68-L pilots were thus used with fresh muni-
cipal solid waste (MSW) shredded to a 40-mm size. After 14 months of landﬁlling, the control has pro-
duced less than 10 NL kg1 DM, which corresponds to around 7% of its biochemical methane potential
(BMP). Nevertheless, on one hand for aerobically pretreated waste, the lag phase before the onset of meth-
anogenesis is signiﬁcantly reduced to 0.9 month compared to more than 1 year for the control. In addition
to that, on average 110 NL kg1 DM (90% of the BMP) is produced within around 6.5 months. On the other
hand, the waste with added bottom ash shows a slight improvement of the lag phase over the control for
one of the duplicate: 6.1 months of lag phase. At this stage, on average of 26 NL kg1 DM waste are
detected (22% of the BMP) no ﬁnal conclusion concerning the impact of bottom ashes could be made.
The data obtained for the leachate parameters agrees with the observations on methane production. Sta-
tistical correlation study shows that the two components of the corrected PCA interpret 76% of the vari-
ability of the data: SUVA (speciﬁc UV absorbance at 254 nm) and HPI (% of hydrophilic compounds)
are identiﬁed as interesting parameters for following up the biodegradation in landﬁll conditions.

1. Introduction
According to the French legislation (Arrêté ministériel du 09/09/
1997), monitoring and treatment of both leachate and biogas pro-
duced in the landﬁll are obligatory during site operation and extend
for an aftercare period of at least 30 years. This legislation joins, at
the European level, the council directive 99/31/EC which also aims
at preventing or reducing as far as possible the negative impacts on
the environment from landﬁlling through the introduction of strin-
gent technical requirements such as waste treatment. And more re-
cently the European Directive 2008/99/CE promotes the increase in
the waste material recovery rate. Unfortunately despite all these
challenges, municipal solid waste (MSW) landﬁlling remains one
of the most common waste treatment processes in France. Pub-
lished data of the French environmental agency (ADEME) show
that, in 2006, 48 million tons of MSW were produced with almost
50% diverted to landﬁlls. It is also the case in Italy where even with
the high rate of selective collection, 40% of the waste goes to the
non-differentiated MSW fraction with an organic content varying
between 20% and 25% (Di Maria et al., 2010). In China, 80% of the
generated MSW is landﬁlled (Yue et al., 2011). In this latter case,
the organic fraction is predominant and leads most of the times
to an acidiﬁcation in the landﬁll and consequently longer lag phases
before methanogenesis and longer periods for the waste (Shao
et al., 2005). In summary worldwide important amounts of organic
matter still go to the landﬁll with important methane and other
green house gas emissions potentials.
In Europe and more speciﬁcally in Austria and Germany, the
mechanical biological treatment (MBT) has been widely used in or-
der to stabilize the waste before landﬁlling. Biostabilization pro-
cesses of 2–6 months have been set up keeping in mind that
according to De Gioannis et al. (2009) between 80% and 91% reduc-
tion of biogas potential can be achieved after 8 and 15 weeks of pre-
treatment respectively. However, in the European Directive 2001/
77/CE, which promotes the increase in the contribution of renew-
able energy sources to electricity production, the biogas produced
by the degradation of waste in the landﬁlls is cited as a source of

renewable energy. Within this new context of increasing environ-
mental concern and promoting renewable energies, it becomes
essential to invest in the optimization of current practices of con-
ventional landﬁlling and thus modify the approach to the MBT.
Waste pretreatment becomes again one key factor with high poten-
tial. An interesting consequence has thus been the shift towards a
new MBT concept in Italy which reduces the biostabilization period
to 2–4 weeks only (Scaglia et al., 2011). Even for the bioreactor
landﬁll, also in Italy, waste pretreatment is looked at to reduce
operational problems on site and increase the biogas production
(Di Maria and Valentini, 2011). In China, waste pretreatment is also
being approached as the solution to limit acidogenesis and thus
shorten the lag phase in the landﬁll (Yue et al., 2011).
In this perspective this work, part of the project BIOPTIME (ANR
Precodd 2006) funded by the French National Agency on Research,
focuses on studying two types of pretreatments before landﬁlling:
addition of bottom ashes and aerobic pretreatment.
On one hand, bottom ashes are the heterogeneous solid resi-
dues remaining after municipal solid waste (MSW) incineration.
According to the French Environment and Energy Management
Agency (ADEME), 21% were co-disposed with MSW in landﬁlls in
2002, which represent more than 500,000 tons of these residues.
In addition to the fact that important amounts of bottom ashes
are available, mixing those particles with the waste is expected
to generate buffering capacity in the medium due to the alkalinity
of the bottom ashes. This latter can positively impact the enzy-
matic activity of the microorganisms (Lo et al., 2009) thus acceler-
ating the process of biodegradation (Wang et al., 2009). In addition
to that, the hydrolysis of polymers contained in the waste results in
the production of volatile fatty acids that may cause a drop in the
pH (Siegert and Banks, 2005; Wang et al., 2009). Generally, the
consumption of VFA by methanogenic microorganisms counterbal-
ances this accumulation but if the rate of hydrolysis is too strong,
the pH may drop, inhibiting the overall degradation process. The
alkalinity brought by the bottom ashes may therefore counterbal-
ance the acidity generated during the initial fermentation stage
and thus accelerate the overall degradation process (Johnson and
Furrer, 2002; Guimaraes et al., 2006; Polettini et al., 2007).
On the other hand, Johansen and Bakke (2006) mentioned that
even the injection of small amounts of air allows an increase in the
hydrolysis rate of waste due to the aerobic activity of the microor-
ganisms. Therefore, the major target of the aerobic pretreatment is
the initiation of the hydrolysis that could be a limiting kinetic step
for this type of waste. Literature data shows that lignocellulosic
compounds, highly abundant in waste, are not easily degradable
by microorganisms (Jash and Ghosh, 1996; Ress et al., 1998). The
aerobic pretreatment aims thus at initiating the degradation of
those types of compounds. Enzymes produced by aerobic fungi
can attack the cellulose ﬁbers and allow a better colonization
and by that a better degradation of the waste when this latter is
placed under anaerobic conditions.
Taking in account these advantages, this work studies the effect
of each pretreatment on the onset and kinetics of methanogenesis
and the leachate quality. It focuses also on the correlation between
methane production and the different parameters measured in the
leachate produced in order to ﬁnd adequate follow-up parameters
of the methanogenesis.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Experimental setup
The pilots used in this study are cylindrical units made up of
opaque polyvinyl chloride (PVC) (Fig. 1). They are all air tight with
a total working volume of 68 L (H = 63 cm and D = 37 cm). The
leachate collection system for the pilots is made up of an inclined
bottom and a stainless steel perforated plate which allows the
downward ﬂow of the leachate from the waste (Fig. 1). At the low-
est point of the leachate reservoir, a valve allows the easy collec-
tion of the leachate.
The cover of each pilot is equipped with ﬁve valves: a pressure
control valve, a valve connecting the inner atmosphere to a micro-
gas chromatograph (Varian CP-4900), a valve connected to a drum-
type gas meter (Ritter model TG1), a 3-way valve that allows
injecting liquid into the system without any gas entry and ﬁnally
a security valve.
During the experiments, the pilots are placed in a room at 35 C.
The inner atmosphere of each pilot is constantly kept in slight
overpressure. The pressure control valve of every pilot is connected
to an automatic system that whenever the pressure builds up in
the system and reaches 0.3 bar, the pressure opens till the pressure
drops to 0.1 bar.
In this study the used feedstock is a fresh MSW obtained from
an industrial municipal solid waste treatment plant, where it is
crushed with an industrial mill and then screened to obtain the
fraction under 40 mm. After this pretreatment, the waste is sent
on the same day from the industrial plant and placed directly in
the 68-L pilots or sent for aerobic pretreatment. On average,
14.2 ± 0.8 kg of dry matter (DM) were placed in each pilot with al-
most 50% moisture content. The initial VSs (volatile solids) content
was measured at 52 ± 5% of TS (total solids). Its average biochem-
ical methane potential (BMP) was measured at 140 NL CH4/kg dry
matter (DM) of waste. For all samples, the BMP was determined on
dried and grinded samples. All tests were performed in 0.5 L ser-
ums bottles, in mesophilic conditions and with a substrate/inocu-
lum ratio ranging from 0.2 to 0.5 g of VSsubstrate per gram of
VSinoculum. The cumulated biogas production was measured during
44 days and analyzed by micro-gas chromatography. The tests
were carried out in duplicate. More details about the method are
available in Angelidaki et al. (2009) and Hansen et al. (2004).
In addition to that, Table 1 presents the general composition of
the MSW according to the guidelines of the national household
characterization survey conducted in 1993 (ADEME, 1995).
Previous experiments (data not published) have shown that
when the waste is placed in the pilots even at 50% humidity, the
onset of methanogenesis did not occur for a control even after
1 year of landﬁlling. It was therefore decided to saturate the waste
at its placement in the pilot with a leachate collected from a land-
ﬁll operated by Veolia Environnement in the Ile de France region
(78). Over 30 L of fresh leachate were injected in each pilot. They
were kept in contact with the waste for 2 h and then drained by
gravity; almost 70% of the injected leachate was recovered by

gravity. Later the headspace was purged with nitrogen in order to
make sure of complete anaerobic conditions. It is important to note
that the remaining leachate was recovered from the pilots over an
average period of 2 months following saturation/desaturation.
Afterwards, almost no leachate was recovered from the pilots.
Therefore 500 mL of distilled water are injected in each pilot on a
monthly basis for the waste not to dry out since on-site the waste
that has already been placed in an active cell still receives water
from rainfall and humidity from newly added waste. In addition
to that with the added water regularly, it is sure to have a mini-
mum amount of leachate for analysis.
2.2. Pretreatments
As mentioned earlier, two types of pretreatment are tested in
this work. On one hand, for the bottom ash addition, the optimal
amount has been previously optimized within the context of the
project (Boulanger et al., 2009a); the rate of addition was found
to be less than 15% of bottom ashes per kg of dry waste. In this
case, bottom ashes were mixed with the MSW in an automatic
rotating drum reactor until homogenization of the mixture and
then the mixture was placed in the 68-L reactors. Note that no
VS content is brought in by the bottom ashes; these incineration
particles are mainly made up of mineral content.
On the other hand, the aerobic pretreatment consisted of a com-
posting phase which corresponds to a stage during which the deg-
radation occurs aerobically (air is forced into the waste matrix).
This step is accompanied by a complete monitoring of the gas
emissions mainly those of carbons such as total hydrocarbons
(THCs) and carbon dioxide as well as the nitrogenous compounds.
The composting process was kept for less than 5 days in order to
achieve a total carbon loss level between 10% and 20% carbon loss
per kg of dry waste. The level of aerobic pretreatment has already
been optimized on a reconstituted MSW in the 68-L pilots in
Mansour et al. (2010).
In total, six pilots are followed: a control ‘‘C’’, two duplicate
pilots with an aerobic pretreatment ‘‘A_x’’ and ‘‘A_y’’, two duplicate
pilots with added bottom ashes ‘‘B_x’’ and ‘‘B_y’’ and one pilot with
both an aerobic pretreatment and addition of bottom ashes ‘‘AB’’.
In fact, the pilot AB is used to see if there is any synergistic effect
of both pretreatments.
2.3. Gas analysis and modeling
The volume of the biogas produced is measured using a drum-
type Ritter gasmeter (type TG1) and the quality of the biogas is
determined using a Varian micro-gas chromatograph (CP 4900)
with helium as a carrier gas. Percentages of CH4, H2S, CO2, O2, N2
and H2 are measured on a daily basis.
In order to characterize and compare the control and the differ-
ent pretreatment pilots, cumulative production curves are mod-
eled using a modiﬁed Gompertz equation (Zwietering et al.,
1990; Lay et al., 1998a,b; Zhu et al., 2009). The modiﬁed equation
is described below:

2.4. Leachate analysis
An extensive follow-up of the leachate is conducted on a
monthly basis on all pilots for nine different parameters. Both pH
(CyberScan pH 510, Eutech instrument) and conductivity (Tetra-
com 325, LF 538) are followed with time. Dissolved organic carbon
(DOC) is measured using a TEKMAR DOHRMANN (model Phoenix
8000) carbon analyzer and chemical oxygen demand (COD) using
the closed reﬂux colorimetric method (NFT 90-101). UV 254 nm is
measured using a doubled-beam spectrophotometer (PharmaSpec
1700 from Shimadzu) with 1 cm-long quartz cells. Total alkalinity
(TA) and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) are evaluated through a poten-
tiometric dosage. Ammonia ðNHþ
4 Þ is measured using a colorimetric
method with a multi-parameter analyzer AQ2 from Seal analytical
and total nitrogen (Nt) according to the French norm NF EN 25663
T90-110.
In addition to the parameters mentioned above, the character-
ization of the organic matter is carried out by fractionation accord-
ing to the hydrophobic character of the organic molecules
(Weishaar et al., 2003). Humic-like compounds are eliminated by
ﬁltration through 0.45 lm membrane. Then, humic-like acids
(HA) are separated by acidiﬁcation at pH 2 and ﬁltration through
a 0.45 lm membrane. The samples are passed through DAX-8 and
XAD-4 resins in series to separate according to the hydrophobic
character the following fractions: hydrophobic-like substances
(HPO), transphilic-like substances (TPH) and hydrophilic-like
substances (HPI).
Based on the data above three indices are calculated. The SUVA
index (the ratio of the UV absorbance to the DOC) is calculated to
estimate the aromatic character of the organic molecules which re-
ﬂects the state of biodegradation of the waste matter. The HS which
is the sum of the HA and the HPO corresponds to the part of hydro-
phobiccompounds.Theycan beconsideredas weaklybiodegradable
organiccompounds.Finallytheratio HA/FA,inwhichFAstandsfor
fulvic like-acid and is assimilated to the HPO fractions, is calculated.
HA/FA is used to evaluate the state of stabilization of the waste: the
higher the ratio, the higher the state of stabilization.

2.5. Statistical approach
All statistical analyses are preceded by the determining if the
data follow a normal distribution using the Shaphiro–Wilk test.
Since it was not the case, all data were normalized using the
Box–Cox method (Box and Cox, 1964). Given the nature of the data,
it was most suitable to conduct a principal component analysis
(PCA) for the interpretation. It is so because the PCA is an explor-
atory statistical method based a factorial analysis (Jackson, 2003).
It is based on the visualization of the information given in a data
set in the form of scattered points in geometrical spaces. The

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Impact on methanogenesis kinetics
Methane production presented below (Fig. 2) is given in terms
of NL of methane per kg of DM of waste since added bottom ashes
consist mainly of mineral matter that does not contribute to the
methane potential of the waste; this presentation allows a compar-
ison of the different pilots on an equal basis.
The ﬁgure above (Fig. 2) shows that the pilots are divided into
two distinct groups: the ﬁrst one corresponds to the three pilots
with the aerobic pretreatment and the second one the control
and the two pilots with added bottom ashes. Results thus show a
signiﬁcant advantage of the aerobic pretreatment over the control
and bottom ashes addition. In 6.5 months of landﬁlling, methane
production is stabilized for the three pilots A_x, A_y and AB;
respectively 98%, 90% and 79% of the initial methane potential
are expressed. Nevertheless these values should be corrected since
the step of saturation/desaturation at the waste placement has

removed some inherent COD of the waste matrix. After conversion
of the COD into methane equivalent, 100%, 100% and 91% of the ini-
tial methane potential (corrected values) are expressed for the
above mentioned pilots. Moreover, it seems that adding bottom
ashes to aerobically treated waste did not have any signiﬁcant im-
pact on the methane production. The differences among the three
pilots could be simply due to experimental errors and most impor-
tantly to the heterogeneity of the waste matrix.
Contrary to the aerobic pretreatment, bottom ash addition did
not show interesting results under unsaturated conditions. After
14 months of landﬁlling, only 28% and 12% of the methane poten-
tial was produced for B_x and B_y respectively (43% and 28% cor-
rected values). Interestingly the pilot B_x shows an onset of the
methanogenesis earlier than that of its duplicate B_y and the con-
trol; an observation that could be explained by the heterogeneity
of the matrix. Unfortunately, the results obtained by Boulanger
et al. (2009a,b), under saturated conditions, in which bottom ash
addition shows very interesting results in terms of kinetics could
not be conﬁrmed with the 68 L-pilots. The action mode of the bot-
tom ashes might thus thrive more under saturated conditions.
Since the methane production of the pilots C, B_x and B_y is in
its early stages, both Vm and Pcm values for these pilots should be
thus taken carefully (Table 2).
The results of the lag phase k show clearly that aerobic pretreat-
ment presents a signiﬁcant advantage over the control and bottom
ash addition. The onset of methanogenesis is on average 0.9 month
after waste placement for the A_x, A_y and AB pilots. It is thus al-
most 11.2 times longer on average for the remaining pilots C, B_x
and B_y taking into account the signiﬁcant difference in k between
the duplicate pilots B_x and B_y (6.1 months vs. 11.4 months).
These observations could be explained by the fact that at least
part of the hydrolysis step takes place during the aerobic pretreat-
ment. Once the waste is placed under anaerobic conditions the
saturation/desaturation with the leachate can remove an important
fraction of the remaining volatile fatty acids of the medium and thus
methanogenesis could start almost immediately. However, for the

remaining pilots C, B_x and B_y, hydrolysis occurs in the pilots and
the waste does not have sufﬁcient inherent buffering capacity to
overcome the acidity: the pH of C and B_y is still below 6 while that
of B_x remained below 6 till the 8th month of the experiment.
For Vm and Pcm, a comparison between the pretreatments
could not be made. Nevertheless within the BIOPTIME project,
Boulanger et al. (2009b) has run tests using the same levels of aer-
obic pretreatment but with reconstituted MSW and under satu-
rated anaerobic conditions in 1 L-reactors. The authors found that
the Vm values recorded at the 68-L scale are comparable to those
presented by under saturated conditions: 1.15 for unsaturated vs.
1.19 for saturated conditions on average. Surprisingly the Pcm val-
ues are higher for the current work: 104 for unsaturated vs. 70 for
saturated conditions; this could be explained by the fact that the
waste used in the 68-L pilots is a real waste with inherent micro-
ﬂora that along with the saturation/desaturation with leachate
step allows a better degradation proﬁle.
3.2. Impact on leachate parameters
From the different parameters only the pH, EC, COD, TA, VFA,
NHþ
4 and SUVA as well as the fractionation will be presented in de-
tails since DOC and COD follow similar proﬁles, the nitrogen re-
leased is mainly in the ammonia form and since SUVA is the
ratio of DOC and UV.
As shown in Fig. 3, the evolution of the pH agrees with the evo-
lution of the methane production presented in Fig. 2. The pH re-
mains below 6 for the control up until 14 months of landﬁlling.
For the pilots A_x, A_y and AB, the pH increases to neutrality be-
tween 2 and 3 months after landﬁlling. The increase to a pH of 7
for B_x appears at month 7 and that for B_y at month 12; these re-
sults show the variability among the duplicates with bottom ash
addition and are in agreement with the variability observed on
methane production for these pilots.
Fig. 4 shows that the decrease of conductivity EC is immediate
for the three pilots with aerobic pretreatment. However, for the
three remaining pilots, one inﬂexion point appears at month 7
for B_x and another at month 12 for B_y. The data thus agree with
the methane produced and the pH values.
The COD data (Fig. 5) show that for the pilots A_x, A_y and AB
the values of COD become almost negligible after 3 months of
landﬁlling; the COD drops on average from 7100 mg O2/kg DM to
480 mg O2/kg DM, that is almost a 15-folds decrease in the COD va-
lue. For B_x the inﬂexion point is apparent at month 7, although
the proﬁle of B_y follows very closely that of the control. This
observation could mean that although a methane production has
started in the pilot B_y, methanogenesis remains in its early stages.
This latter observation is also identical when looking at the evo-
lution of VFA with time for the different pilots (Fig. 6).
For the previous parameters, at least B_x was different from the
control. While when looking into the ammonia concentration
(Fig. 7), one can see only two distinct groups with C, B_x and B_y
on one hand and A_x, A_y and AB on the other hand. In fact, Wens
et al. (2001) and Yuen et al. (1995) indicate that an accumulation of
NHþ
4 can lead to the inhibition of the degradation of the waste. This
inhibition was observed by the authors for concentrations higher
than 1500 mg/L. During the experiments the total quantity of
NHþ
4 remains all the time below this value.
For all data shown so far, no signiﬁcant difference was shown
among the pilots B and C. However, when looking into the TA data
(Fig. 8) an important difference appears for the pilots with bottom
ash addition. The TA for the control remains below 0.7 g CaCO3/L,
however, for the pilots B_x and B_y it shows the highest values:
the bottom ash addition did not have an impact on the pH of the
leachate, however, an important impact on TA could be noticed.
Surprisingly, this observation does not hold true for the pilot AB;
one can assume that the impact of bottom ashes is masked by that
of the aerobic pretreatment.
Finally, Fig. 9 shows the evolution of the SUVA index with time.
The results shown agree with previously published data by
François et al. (2006) and Feuillade et al. (2009). This index is
characteristic of hydrophobic organic molecules as it provides indi-
cations on their aromaticity. Feuillade et al. (2009) considered that
this index increases during waste degradation with values going
from below 10 to above 30 L cm1 g C1. As shown in Fig. 9, the
SUVA index values for aerobically pretreated waste goes from
around 5 to about 23 L cm1 g C1 while those of the remaining
pilots are below 5 L cm1 g C1. It is nevertheless noteworthy to
point the inﬂexion point for B_x that correlates with the onset of
the methanogenesis in this pilot.

3.3. Statistical approach for the correlation between methane
production and leachate parameters
Leachate follow-up of the 68 L pilots has been extensive there-
fore an important objective of this work is to identify leachate
parameters that could be used as indicators of the biodegradation
through a statistical approach.
In this perspective, primary analysis showed that the data did
not follow a normal distribution therefore all parameters were
transformed using the Box–Cox method. Since the data set consisted
of a large number of interrelated variables, the PCA was achieved in
order to reduce the number of the observed variables while retain-
ing as much as possible of the variation present in the data set (Jol-
liffe, 2002). Therefore, a ﬁrst PCA (Fig. 12) was generated using all
the data set. The two principal components of this PCA were able
to interpret in total almost 74% of the total variability of the data.
But the number of parameters was only slightly reduced.
It was therefore decided to conduct another PCA while taking
into account only the data set that corresponds to the stage after
the initiation of the methanogenesis. One major reason is that for
the pilots C, B_x and B_y there was no methane production for
an important period of time, only null values are generated for this
parameter and this can easily distort the analysis.
The second PCA (Fig. 13) reduced thus more signiﬁcantly the
number of variables: SUVA, HS, HPO are directly correlated to
the cumulative CH4 production while EC, pH, UV absorbance and
HPI are negatively correlated. The two components explain still
73% of the variability of the data.
From this analysis, the ﬁrst indicator to be conﬁrmed as a rele-
vant indicator of the biodegradation is SUVA index. However, in or-
der to conﬁrm the correlation between CH4 cum and HPI, the HS
variable was removed as well as two data points from the scores
that distorted the distribution. HPO was also removed since it
did not show an interesting impact on neither components of the
PCA. The two components of the new PCA explain 76% of the
variability and express better the correlation between the two
parameters. This covariance is conﬁrmed by a Coefﬁcient of
Pearson of -0.88 (Fig. 14). HPI is conﬁrmed as an interesting
parameter of follow-up.

4. Conclusions
Aerobic preparation and bottom ash addition have been tested as
pretreatment steps of a French MSW before landﬁlling in 68 L-pilots.
After 14 months of landﬁlling, the control shows no signiﬁcant
production of methane. Nevertheless, on one hand for aerobically
pretreated waste, the lag phase before the onset of methanogenesis
is signiﬁcantly reduced to less than 1 month compared to 1 year for
the control. In addition to that, more than 90%, on average, of the
BMP of the landﬁlled waste is expressed in around 6.5 months. This
is accompanied by an important rate of methane production that
goes up to 1.17 NL CH4 kg1 DM day1. This aerobic pretreatment
has thus proven its efﬁciency and the scaling-up becomes the future
industrial challenge to look into. On the other hand, the waste with
added bottom ash shows a slight improvement of the lag phase over
the control for one of the duplicates (6.1 months vs. 12.6 months for
the control) and of the biogas produced (26% for the bottom ashes
and 7% for the control). At this level of the experiments no ﬁnal con-
clusion could be made for the effect of bottom ashes until stabiliza-
tion of the biogas production.
The results of the leachate follow-up for COD, pH, EC, TA, VFA
and ammonia agree with the results of the methane production.
Using all data sets, the two components of the corrected PCA inter-
pret 76% of the variability of the data. Both the SUVA and the HPI
appear as interesting parameters for following up the biodegrada-
tion in landﬁll conditions.
